statement: Software originates from and remains deeply connected to its domain; the primary purpose of any software system is to serve a specific real-world domain, so design must start there.
To make software fit harmoniously with its domain, developers should model the software as a direct reflection of the domain — capturing its core concepts, elements, and relationships precisely.

A domain model is not a particular diagram but the idea the diagram is intended to convey; it is a rigorously organized, selective abstraction of knowledge drawn from domain experts, not merely what lives in an expert's head.

The model is the internal representation of the target domain and is essential throughout design and development; without an explicit model, complexity becomes unmanageable and software cannot evolve with the domain.
The model must be communicated — through diagrams, writing, and a shared language — because it is the essence of the software and must be understood by both domain experts and developers.

DDD combines design and development practice so that design accelerates development and feedback from development continuously enhances the design, addressing the one-way information flow weakness of waterfall approaches.

Domain knowledge must be built collaboratively between software specialists and domain experts through sustained dialogue; domain experts possess the essential domain knowledge, while software specialists provide the analytical structure needed to transform it into a model.

In early conversations with domain experts, the software specialist should ask questions to uncover essential concepts, extract key vocabulary, and identify the relationships between domain elements — even if those concepts initially emerge unpolished and disorganized.

The communication between domain experts and software specialists is bidirectional: domain experts supply knowledge, and the analytical perspective of software specialists helps surface key domain concepts and construct the structure of future discussions.

The domain model is created jointly by software specialists and domain experts; it is the place where these two areas of expertise meet, making the process time-consuming but necessary because the software must ultimately blend perfectly with the domain.

A fundamental communication barrier exists between developers (who think in classes, patterns, and algorithms) and domain experts (who speak in domain-specific jargon); bridging this gap requires a deliberately constructed shared language.

When terminology used in day-to-day team discussions is disconnected from the terminology embedded in the code, the most precise expressions of the domain emerge in a transient form that is never captured and team members cannot share knowledge reliably.
condition: team discussion terminology is disconnected from code terminology

statement: A core DDD principle: use a language based on the model as the backbone of all team communication; this language — the Ubiquitous Language — must be used consistently in all forms of communication including speech, writing, diagrams, and code.
A change in the Ubiquitous Language must become a change in the domain model, and vice versa; the language and the model are strongly interconnected and must evolve in lockstep.

Domain experts should object to terms or structures that fail to convey domain understanding, while developers should watch for ambiguity or inconsistency in design; both sides bear responsibility for the integrity of the Ubiquitous Language.

The Ubiquitous Language is built through collaborative design sessions in which team members use key domain terms in bold, correct one another, and gradually converge on a shared vocabulary; all team members must stay focused on essentials and avoid private jargon.

Developers should implement the main concepts of the model in code — giving classes names drawn directly from the Ubiquitous Language — so that the code expresses the model, becomes more readable, and reproduces the language accurately.

Small focused diagrams covering a subset of the model, supplemented by explanatory text for behavior and constraints, are more effective than a single large diagram of the entire model, which typically becomes too cluttered to communicate clearly.

Documents used to communicate the model must remain in sync with the model; outdated documents that use incorrect language and no longer reflect the current model are not helpful and should be avoided.

When a separate analysis model is created without input from developers and then handed off for implementation, a growing divide opens between model and code; developers adapt or replace the model, domain knowledge is lost in translation, and the software drifts from what the model intended.
condition: analysis model is created without developer input and handed off

statement: Analysts working independently cannot foresee all defects and intricacies of the domain; important details about object persistence, performance, and invariants are only discovered during design and implementation, making pure analysis models impractical.

Domain modeling and design must be closely related: the model should be constructed with an eye toward software and design considerations, and developers must be included in the modeling process to ensure the model can actually be implemented.

Those who write the code must know the model well and feel responsible for its integrity; a change to the code implies a change to the model, and refactoring code to the point where it no longer expresses the model is a design failure.

Any technical person contributing to the model must spend time touching the code, and every developer must be involved in some level of discussion about the model and have contact with domain experts; model ideas must be exchanged through the Ubiquitous Language.

A software system should be designed so that a portion of it literally reflects the domain model, making the mapping obvious; if the central part of the design does not map to the domain model, the model has little value and the software's correctness is suspect.

A complex application should be partitioned into four conceptual layers: User Interface, Application, Domain, and Infrastructure; each layer depends only on layers below it, and the Domain Layer is isolated from UI, application, and infrastructure concerns.

Mixing domain-related code with other layers makes it extremely difficult to understand and modify business logic; changes to the UI can accidentally alter business rules, and implementing model-driven objects becomes impractical.
condition: domain code is mixed with other layers

statement: Concentrating all domain model code in a single isolated layer — free from display, storage, and application task responsibilities — allows the model to evolve into a rich representation capable of capturing essential business knowledge.

An Entity is a domain object defined by its thread of identity and continuity across states, rather than by its attribute values; two objects with the same attributes are not the same Entity if they have different identities.

When an object is distinguished by its identity rather than its attributes, make identity primary to its model definition; define a means of distinguishing each object regardless of its form or history, and define an operation that produces a unique result per object.
condition: object is distinguished by identity rather than attributes

statement: Identity for an Entity may be an attribute, a combination of attributes, a specially created attribute, or even a behavior; the key requirement is that two objects with the same identity must be considered the same by the system, and mistaken identity leads to data corruption.
A Value Object describes certain aspects of a domain element through its attributes alone and has no identity; it is not tracked and does not need to be uniquely identified, unlike an Entity.

Value Objects should be made immutable: created with a constructor and never modified during their lifetime; when a different value is needed, a new Value Object is created rather than modifying the existing one.
Immutable Value Objects can be safely shared; if a shareable Value Object were mutable, changes to it by one consumer would inadvertently affect all other consumers referencing the same object.

Attributes grouped into a Value Object should form a conceptual whole; for example, street, city, and state conceptually belong together as an Address Value Object rather than as separate attributes on a Customer Entity.

When an important domain behavior does not naturally belong to any Entity or Value Object — because it represents a significant action involving multiple objects — it should be declared as a Service rather than forced into an existing domain object.
condition: domain behavior does not naturally belong to any Entity or Value Object

statement: A Service has three defining characteristics: the operation refers to a domain concept that does not naturally belong to an Entity or Value Object, the operation refers to other objects in the domain, and the operation is stateless.

Services should not replace operations that naturally belong on domain objects; a Service should only be created when such an operation stands out as an important concept in the domain, and it should be defined using the Ubiquitous Language.

The domain layer must remain isolated from infrastructure and application concerns; Services at the application and domain layers serve different purposes, and deciding which layer a Service belongs to requires careful consideration of whether the operation is conceptually part of the domain.

When a model grows large, it must be organized into Modules that group related concepts and tasks; understanding the interaction between Modules provides a higher-level view of the system before diving into internal details.

Modules should be chosen to tell the story of the system with a cohesive set of concepts, maximizing internal cohesion and minimizing coupling between modules; Module names should become part of the Ubiquitous Language and reflect insight into the domain.

Modules should be allowed to evolve with the project rather than kept frozen; when a Module design mistake is found it is better to change the Module than to find workarounds, even though Module refactoring is more expensive than class refactoring.

An Aggregate is a cluster of associated domain objects treated as a single unit for data changes; it has a boundary separating inside objects from outside, and a single root Entity through which all external access must pass.

Only the Aggregate root is accessible from outside the boundary; external objects may only hold persistent references to the root, not to internal objects, so all changes to internal objects are mediated and controlled by the root.

Aggregates enforce invariants: because external objects can only change the root, and the root controls all changes to internal objects, invariants can be reliably maintained across the Aggregate; deleting the root removes all internal objects, guaranteeing referential integrity.

Repositories should only be provided for Aggregate roots; querying the database should return only root objects, with internal objects obtained through traversal associations rather than direct queries.
The root Entity has global identity and is responsible for maintaining invariants; internal Entities of an Aggregate have only local identity, meaningful only within the Aggregate boundary.

To reduce complexity, associations in a model should be minimized: remove non-essential associations, reduce multiplicity by adding constraints where possible, and convert bidirectional associations to unidirectional ones where conceptually justified.

When creating a complex Aggregate or object requires significant knowledge of its internal structure and invariants, a Factory should be used to encapsulate that creation logic; placing complex creation in a constructor or in the client breaks encapsulation and leaks domain knowledge outside the domain layer.
condition: object creation requires significant knowledge of internal structure and invariants

statement: Object creation through a Factory must be atomic: if the creation process cannot complete properly, an exception should be raised to ensure no partially-created, invalid object is returned; this is especially critical for Aggregates where all invariants must be enforced at creation time.

A Factory Method added to an Aggregate root is suitable for creating objects that belong inside that Aggregate; a dedicated Factory class is more appropriate when the construction of an Aggregate involves a complex series of steps or the creation of many related objects simultaneously.

A simple constructor is sufficient when construction is not complex, does not involve creating other objects, and when the client is interested in the implementation; Factories are needed only when object creation is a major, knowledge-intensive operation.

Reconstituting a persisted object from a database is fundamentally different from creating a new one: the reconstituted object already has an identity and invariant violations should be handled as repair rather than as exceptions, whereas a fresh object creation must fail loudly on any invariant breach.

A Repository encapsulates all logic needed to obtain references to pre-existing domain objects; domain objects should obtain needed references through the Repository rather than by accessing the infrastructure directly, keeping the model clear and focused on domain concepts.

Only provide Repositories for Aggregate roots that actually need direct access; the Repository interface should be a pure domain model interface even though its implementation may contain infrastructure details, shielding clients from persistence technology.

Allowing clients to access the database directly causes domain logic to migrate into queries and client code, turns Entities and Value Objects into mere data containers, and makes the model irrelevant; a Repository prevents this by keeping the domain focus intact.

A Repository provides an interface that gives the illusion of an in-memory collection of all objects of a given type; it should expose methods to add, remove, and select objects by criteria, encapsulating the actual storage and query technology completely.

Factories create new objects from scratch, while Repositories find and reconstitute already-existing objects; to add a new object to the system, it should be created by the Factory first and then given to the Repository for storage.

Refactoring is the process of redesigning code to make it better without changing application behavior; it is done in small, controllable steps and requires automated tests to verify that no functionality is broken.

Sophisticated domain models are seldom developed except through an iterative refactoring process with close involvement of domain experts and developers who are interested in learning about the domain.

Beyond technical code-quality refactoring, there is a second kind driven by new insight into the domain — when a relationship between elements is discovered or a concept becomes clearer, those insights must be incorporated into the design through refactoring.

Code should express not only what it does but why it does it; expressive, readable code that captures the substance of the model is the goal of domain-driven refactoring, not merely syntactically clean code.

A deep model sloughs off the superficial and captures the essential; starting from nouns and verbs produces only a shallow model — the model must be iteratively refined toward deeper and deeper insight to become useful.

A breakthrough in design occurs when implicit concepts are made explicit: when a concept that was being used to explain other concepts is recognized as a key domain concept deserving its own class or relationship in the model.

Implicit concepts can be discovered by listening carefully to the language used during modeling: key concepts emerge in the Ubiquitous Language and should be looked for there; awkwardness in a design section often signals a missing key concept.

Apparent contradictions between domain experts or between requirements often turn out to be different perspectives on the same concept; reconciling them can surface important implicit concepts and improve the model.

Constraints should be made explicit by extracting invariant logic into separate, named methods or Constraint objects, making it clear that an operation is subject to a specific rule and allowing the constraint to grow in complexity without cluttering the host object.

A Specification is an object used to test whether another object satisfies a certain criterion; it encapsulates complex business rules that would otherwise bloat an Entity or migrate to the application layer, keeping them in the domain layer where they belong.
Simple Specifications testing single rules can be composed into composite Specifications expressing complex business rules; this keeps the rules explicit, cohesive, and readable at the point of use.

In large multi-team projects, striving to maintain one large unified model for the entire enterprise will not work; instead, the model should be consciously divided into several well-integrated smaller models, each with a clearly delimited boundary and precisely defined relationships.
The internal consistency of a model is called unification; without it, terms become ambiguous or contradictory across the codebase, and the model loses its value as a shared conceptual framework.

A Bounded Context defines the scope within which a specific domain model applies; its boundaries must be explicitly set in terms of team organization, application boundaries, code bases, and database schemas so that the model stays strictly consistent within those bounds.

A Bounded Context is not a Module; a Bounded Context provides the logical frame within which the model evolves and encompasses Modules, whereas Modules are used to organize the elements within a model.

When different teams work on the same model, changes to the model may break existing functionality; using multiple Bounded Contexts lets each team work freely within their own context, keeping their model pure, consistent, and independently refinable.
condition: multiple teams work on the same model

statement: Even within a Bounded Context, the model can fragment as team members add duplicated code or make changes without fully understanding the model; Continuous Integration is a necessary process within a Bounded Context to merge and test code frequently and keep the model unified.

Continuous Integration within a Bounded Context requires a merge procedure (daily for small teams), an automated build, and an automated test suite that is run on every build; Continuous Integration applies only within a Bounded Context and does not address relationships between neighboring contexts.

A Context Map is a document — diagram or written — that outlines all Bounded Contexts in a project and the relationships between them; every team member must share and understand it so that integration boundaries are clear and overlapping contexts can be avoided.

Each Bounded Context should be named using the Ubiquitous Language; a common practice is to define each context, create Modules for it, and use a naming convention in the code to indicate which Bounded Context each Module belongs to.

A Shared Kernel designates a specific subset of the domain model — and the associated code and database design — that two teams agree to share; changes to this subset require consultation with both teams and must not be made unilaterally.

Teams using a Shared Kernel must integrate their changes to the kernel frequently (at least weekly), maintain a shared test suite that both teams run against the kernel, and communicate all changes to each other promptly.

When one subsystem heavily depends on another but not vice versa, they are in a Customer-Supplier relationship; the customer team presents requirements and the supplier team sets the timetable, with the schedule driven by the supplier but the interface ultimately meeting the customer's needs.

In a Customer-Supplier relationship, jointly developed automated acceptance tests should validate the interface contract; adding these tests to the supplier's continuous integration suite lets the supplier make changes confidently without risking side effects for the customer's application.

A Customer-Supplier relationship requires management support to work; when the supplier team has no motivation to support the customer team's needs, the customer team must protect itself — either through a conformist stance, an Anticorruption Layer, or by going Separate Ways.
condition: supplier team has no motivation to support customer

statement: An Anticorruption Layer isolates the client model from an external or legacy model; it translates between the two models so the client model remains pure and consistent, presenting external concepts in the client's own terms and preventing external model corruption from leaking in.

The Anticorruption Layer is best implemented as a Service from the client model's perspective, backed by a Facade wrapping the external system and an Adapter that translates between the two systems; a Translator object handles data conversion between the contexts.

When the benefits of integration between two subsystems are not worth the coordination effort, the Separate Ways pattern applies: each subsystem develops its own model independently with no sharing, and integration between them is not pursued; models developed separately are very difficult to re-integrate later.
condition: integration benefits do not justify coordination cost

statement: When a subsystem must be integrated with many other subsystems, rather than creating a custom translation layer for each, define a protocol that gives access to the subsystem as a set of Services; this Open Host Service protocol should be expanded for general integration needs while one-off translators handle idiosyncratic special cases.
condition: subsystem must integrate with many others

statement: Distillation of a large model means identifying the Core Domain — the essence of the application's unique business value — and separating it from Generic Subdomains that, while necessary, are not the primary focus of the project.

The Core Domain should be made small, explicitly highlighted to distinguish it from supporting code, and staffed with the best available developers; if the core business logic is poorly designed or implemented, all other parts of the system provide little value.

Generic Subdomains should be factored out into separate Modules with lower development priority than the Core Domain; teams should consider off-the-shelf solutions or published models for Generic Subdomains rather than investing scarce core-team resources in them.

The Core Domain of one system may become a Generic Subdomain of another; identifying the correct Core is context-dependent and requires understanding the unique business purpose of the specific system being built.

Generic Subdomains can be implemented in four ways: using an off-the-shelf solution, outsourcing to another team, adopting an existing published model, or building in-house; each option has trade-offs around integration effort, dependency, and control.

Evans' practical advice for applying DDD: stay hands-on (modelers must code), anchor abstract thinking in concrete scenarios, avoid applying DDD everywhere (draw a context map to decide where to push DDD), and expect to experiment and make mistakes because modeling is a creative process.
